content: The references provided include a wide range of studies and reviews focusing on the use of dried blood samples for the detection and monitoring of viral infections such as hepatitis B (HBV), hepatitis C (HCV), and HIV. These studies explore the stability of viral RNA in dried blood spots, their utility in resource-limited settings, and their effectiveness in improving diagnostic access and treatment outcomes. For example, Jardí et al. (2004) and Lira et al. (2009) demonstrated the feasibility of using dried blood samples for quantifying and characterizing HBV DNA, as well as monitoring HBV infections. Similarly, Vinikoor et al. (2015) validated the use of dried blood spots for measuring HBV viral load in Zambia, highlighting their potential in low-resource settings. Abe and Konomi (1998) showed that HCV RNA remains stable in dried serum spots at room temperature, while Bennett et al. (2012) and De Crignis et al. (2010) further validated the detection of HCV RNA in dried blood spots using advanced molecular techniques like real-time PCR. These findings underscore the practicality of dried blood spots for HCV diagnosis and genotyping, even in challenging environments. Soullier et al. (2016) emphasized the role of dried blood spots in expanding access to HCV screening, diagnosis, and treatment monitoring, particularly in underserved populations. Santos et al. (2012) and Solmone et al. (2002) also highlighted the reliability of dried blood spots for detecting HCV RNA in chronically infected patients, supporting their integration into public health strategies. Several studies, such as those by Craine et al. (2015) and Hickman et al. (2008), investigated the use of dried blood spot testing to increase hepatitis C antibody testing uptake in high-risk populations, including individuals in prison settings and people who inject drugs. These studies demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach in improving diagnostic rates and linkage to care. Other research, such as that by Hutchinson et al. (2015) and McLeod et al. (2014), explored the impact of national action plans and public health policies on hepatitis C testing and treatment access, with dried blood spot testing playing a pivotal role in these initiatives. In addition to viral hepatitis, the references also include studies on the integration of care for co-infections like HIV and HCV, as well as the role of community health workers and task-shifting strategies in improving access to care in resource-limited settings. For instance, studies by Grebely et al. (2010) and Crawford and Bath (2013) highlighted the importance of multidisciplinary care models and peer support in optimizing HCV treatment for people who inject drugs. Overall, these studies collectively demonstrate the utility of dried blood spot testing as a cost-effective, reliable, and scalable tool for improving the diagnosis and management of viral infections, particularly in underserved and resource-constrained settings. They also emphasize the importance of integrating innovative diagnostic methods into broader public health strategies to enhance access to care and treatment outcomes.
